posts.title: Re-filing the Past
posts.sourceText: We often think of time as three filing cabinets: one for the past, one for the present, and one for the future. It seems obvious that files from the past belong in the past cabinet. But somewhere along the way, most of us make a serious filing error: we take files marked past and slip them into the cabinet marked future. So when we look ahead, the cabinet we expect to hold possibility is already crammed full of history. Little by little, we’ve been filling our future with our past—leaving no room for what could be. The breakthrough comes when we notice this error. When we take the past out of the future and return it to its rightful place. Only then does the future become truly empty—ready to be created.
posts.contentMarkdown:
We often think of time as three filing cabinets: one for the past, one for the present, and one for the future.

It seems obvious that files from the past belong in the past cabinet. But somewhere along the way, most of us make a serious filing error: we take files marked *past* and slip them into the cabinet marked *future*.

So when we look ahead, the cabinet we expect to hold possibility is already crammed full of history.

Little by little, we’ve been filling our future with our past—leaving no room for what could be.

The breakthrough comes when we notice this error: when we take the past out of the future and return it to its rightful place.

**Only then does the future become truly empty—ready to be created.**
posts.seoTitle: Re-filing the Past: Making Room for the Future | WECARE.DIGITAL
posts.metaDescription: When the future is filled with the past, possibility gets crowded out. Re-file the past so the future can become empty and ready to be created.

posts.title: Eradicating Prejudice
posts.sourceText: To be free of prejudice means letting go of our fixed opinions about others—no matter how attached we are to them. It means giving up the need to be right, and instead offering the generosity and grace of a fresh, unprejudiced start in our eyes.

posts.seoTitle: Eradicating Prejudice: A Fresh Start in Our Eyes | WECARE.DIGITAL
posts.metaDescription: To be free of prejudice is to let go of fixed opinions, give up the need to be right, and offer another person a fresh start in our eyes.

posts.title: Beat Yesterday
posts.sourceText: We don’t have to conquer the world. We just have to beat yesterday. A little better than we were twenty-four hours ago. Then again tomorrow. And the day after that. Progress isn’t always about heroics. More often, it’s about showing up—consistently.

Progress isn’t always about heroics. More often, it’s about showing up—consistently.
posts.seoTitle: Beat Yesterday: Progress Through Consistency | WECARE.DIGITAL
posts.metaDescription: Progress is not always heroic. Sometimes it is simply being a little better than yesterday and showing up consistently again tomorrow.

posts.title: Transformation Tourism
posts.sourceText: I bought the diet book—then ate my usual foods. I filled the prescription—then left the pills untouched. I took the course… well, I watched the videos… but never did the exercises. Looking isn’t changing. Tourism is entertaining, but it’s rarely transformative. If change were easy, you’d already be living it. Real transformation comes from habits. From acting as if. From leaning into the discomfort of becoming someone new.

posts.title: Seven Tips for Becoming Outstanding
posts.sourceText: Be racket-free: Give up being right, even when you know you were. Be powerful: Be straight in your communication and take what you get. Be courageous: Acknowledge your fear (you don't necessarily have to get rid of it) and then act. Be peaceful: Let go of the interpretation that there is something wrong. Be charismatic: Give up trying to get somewhere. Be entirely fulfilled in the present moment. Be enrolling: Share your new possibilities in such a way that others are touched, moved and inspired. Be unreasonable: In expectations of yourself and others beyond what you would think they are capable of.
posts.contentMarkdown:
1. **Be racket-free:** Give up being right, even when you know you were.
2. **Be powerful:** Be straight in your communication and take what you get.
3. **Be courageous:** Acknowledge your fear—you don’t necessarily have to get rid of it—and then act.
4. **Be peaceful:** Let go of the interpretation that there is something wrong.
5. **Be charismatic:** Give up trying to get somewhere. Be entirely fulfilled in the present moment.
6. **Be enrolling:** Share your new possibilities in such a way that others are touched, moved, and inspired.
7. **Be unreasonable:** Set expectations of yourself and others beyond what you would think they are capable of.
posts.seoTitle: Seven Tips for Becoming Outstanding | WECARE.DIGITAL
posts.metaDescription: Seven source distinctions on being racket-free, powerful, courageous, peaceful, charismatic, enrolling, and unreasonable.

posts.title: Choosing vs. Deciding
posts.sourceText: Deciding is related to other "*cide" words (suicide, insecticide, genocide) and is the result of applying reason to eliminate alternatives, effectively killing them. Usually, a single thing is left, and that becomes the decision. Choosing is about making a choice purely for the sake of choosing, not applying reason, not applying logic, not removing or disqualifying the other choices. "I choose to believe ..." or "I choose to trust ..." adding "because" makes it a reason. By using reason, one then absolves oneself from responsibility for the choice, and it becomes the fault of the reason or the reasoning process if it fails. Choice demands responsibility for making the choice.
posts.contentMarkdown:
Deciding is related to other “-cide” words and is the result of applying reason to eliminate alternatives. Usually, a single thing is left, and that becomes the decision.

Choosing is about making a choice purely for the sake of choosing—not applying reason, not applying logic, not removing or disqualifying the other choices.

“I choose to believe…” or “I choose to trust…”

Adding “because” makes it a reason.

By using reason, one then absolves oneself from responsibility for the choice, and it becomes the fault of the reason or the reasoning process if it fails.

**Choice demands responsibility for making the choice.**
posts.seoTitle: Choosing vs. Deciding | WECARE.DIGITAL
posts.metaDescription: A distinction between deciding by eliminating alternatives through reason and choosing freely while taking responsibility for the choice.

posts.title: Love
posts.sourceText: I love you” is an illusion. The whole struggle that one through to achieve love, to get love, to have love, to be loved, to love each other. The fastest way to destroy love is to make a goal out of it because people who are trying to be loved come from a place that they’re not loved. And people who are trying to love come from a place that they don’t love. And if you take the barriers out of the way, if you take those things that you didn’t take responsibility for in your life out of the way, what you have left is love. And that’s the whole story about love. Love is.
posts.contentMarkdown:
In this distinction, “I love you” is treated as an illusion when love becomes something to achieve, get, have, receive, or produce.

The fastest way to destroy love is to make a goal out of it, because people trying to be loved come from a place that they’re not loved, and people trying to love come from a place that they don’t love.

If you take the barriers out of the way—if you take responsibility for what has been left in the way—what you have left is love.

**Love is.**
posts.seoTitle: Love: When Love Is No Longer a Goal | WECARE.DIGITAL
posts.metaDescription: A source distinction on love: making love a goal creates struggle; remove the barriers and take responsibility for what is in the way.
